answers.U2-S1: Nature prepares for the next growing season well before the current one ends; new buds, seeds and eggs form in late summer and fall, ready for spring.
answers.U2-S2: To correct a popular but mistaken idea: the new bud forms in the old leaf's axil long before leaves fall, so it rarely pushes them off.
answers.U2-S3: A playful, humorous personification, treating trees that hold dead leaves as indecisive or slovenly people unable to finish with something.
answers.U2-S4: Dropping old leaves is an active act needing a healthy tree's energy; a weak or suddenly killed tree just keeps its withered leaves on the branches.
answers.U2-S5: Beginning; the start or origin of the next season's growth.
answers.U2-S6: He partly agrees that next season's life starts early, but says the real start comes even earlier, in late summer when new tree buds form.
answers.U2-S7: Because, like eggs, they already contain fully formed future life, packed and protected, waiting only for spring's warmth to hatch or open them.
answers.U2-S8: Each season produces and prepares the next; the growth of the coming season is begun and formed during the current one.
answers.U2-S9: His own direct observation of nature, inviting readers to examine leaves, cut open buds, and look at trees themselves.
answers.U2-S10: It sums up the passage's main idea in a closing metaphor: nature always prepares for spring before winter arrives.
